### 6.5.7 Future Monitoring Roadmap

#### 6.5.7.1 Phase 1: Basic Observability (If Needed)

**Estimated Effort:** 4-8 hours  
**Prerequisites:** System scope expansion beyond localhost testing

**Implementation Steps:**

| Step | Task | Effort | Output |
|------|------|--------|--------|
| 1 | Add request logging | 1-2 hours | Log all HTTP requests with method, path, timestamp |
| 2 | Add error handling | 2-3 hours | Try-catch blocks, process error handlers |
| 3 | Add health endpoint | 1 hour | `GET /health` returns 200 OK with status |
| 4 | Environment variables | 1-2 hours | Configurable host and port via process.env |

**Implementation Example:**

```javascript
// Phase 1: Basic observability enhancements (not currently implemented)

const http = require('http');

// Environment variable support
const hostname = process.env.HOST || '127.0.0.1';
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  // Request logging
  const timestamp = new Date().toISOString();
  console.log(`[${timestamp}] ${req.method} ${req.url}`);
  
  try {
    // Health check endpoint
    if (req.url === '/health') {
      res.statusCode = 200;
      res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'healthy', timestamp }));
      return;
    }
    
    // Default endpoint
    res.statusCode = 200;
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
    res.end('Hello, World!\n');
    
    // Response logging
    console.log(`[${timestamp}] Response: ${res.statusCode}`);
  } catch (err) {
    // Error logging
    console.error(`[${timestamp}] ERROR:`, err);
    res.statusCode = 500;
    res.end('Internal Server Error');
  }
});

// Server error handling
server.on('error', (err) => {
  console.error('Server error:', err.message);
  if (err.code === 'EADDRINUSE') {
    console.error(`Port ${port} already in use`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
});

// Process error handling
process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => {
  console.error('Uncaught exception:', err);
  server.close(() => process.exit(1));
});

server.listen(port, hostname, () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
  console.log(`Health check: http://${hostname}:${port}/health`);
});
```

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.3 provides "Recommended implementation path" for production observability including request logging, error tracking, and health endpoints.

#### 6.5.7.2 Phase 2: Metrics and Monitoring (If Production Deployment)

**Estimated Effort:** 20-40 hours  
**Prerequisites:** Phase 1 complete, production deployment planned

**Implementation Steps:**

| Step | Technology | Effort | Purpose |
|------|-----------|--------|---------|
| 1 | Install prom-client | 2-4 hours | Prometheus metrics client library |
| 2 | Instrument application | 4-8 hours | Add metrics collection to code |
| 3 | Create /metrics endpoint | 2-4 hours | Expose metrics for Prometheus scraping |
| 4 | Deploy Prometheus server | 4-8 hours | Set up metrics storage and querying |
| 5 | Configure Grafana | 4-8 hours | Create dashboards for visualization |
| 6 | Set up alert rules | 4-8 hours | Define alerting thresholds |

**Metrics Implementation Example:**

```javascript
// Phase 2: Prometheus metrics (not currently implemented)

const http = require('http');
const promClient = require('prom-client');

// Create Prometheus registry
const register = new promClient.Registry();

// Default metrics (CPU, memory, etc.)
promClient.collectDefaultMetrics({ register });

// Custom metrics
const httpRequestDuration = new promClient.Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'Duration of HTTP requests in seconds',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
  registers: [register]
});

const httpRequestTotal = new promClient.Counter({
  name: 'http_requests_total',
  help: 'Total number of HTTP requests',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
  registers: [register]
});

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const start = Date.now();
  
  // Metrics endpoint
  if (req.url === '/metrics') {
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', register.contentType);
    res.end(register.metrics());
    return;
  }
  
  // Health check endpoint
  if (req.url === '/health') {
    res.statusCode = 200;
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'healthy' }));
    
    // Record metrics
    const duration = (Date.now() - start) / 1000;
    httpRequestDuration.observe({ method: req.method, route: '/health', status: 200 }, duration);
    httpRequestTotal.inc({ method: req.method, route: '/health', status: 200 });
    return;
  }
  
  // Default endpoint
  res.statusCode = 200;
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
  res.end('Hello, World!\n');
  
  // Record metrics
  const duration = (Date.now() - start) / 1000;
  httpRequestDuration.observe({ method: req.method, route: '/', status: 200 }, duration);
  httpRequestTotal.inc({ method: req.method, route: '/', status: 200 });
});

const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
server.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${port}`);
  console.log(`Metrics available at http://localhost:${port}/metrics`);
});
```

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.3 recommends "Export metrics: Prometheus metrics endpoint for Grafana dashboards" as part of production observability roadmap.

## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Testing Strategy Applicability Assessment

#### 6.6.1.1 Applicability Statement

**Detailed Testing Strategy is not applicable for this system.** The hao-backprop-test repository implements a minimal 15-line Node.js HTTP server designed exclusively as test infrastructure for backprop integration validation. This system fundamentally lacks the complexity, production deployment characteristics, and business criticality that would necessitate comprehensive testing practices including unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end testing, and automated test suites.

The system's classification as test-only infrastructure, combined with its minimal functional scope (single static HTTP response), zero external dependencies, stateless architecture, and localhost-only deployment model, renders traditional multi-layered testing strategies both technically unnecessary and economically unjustifiable.

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 1.2.1.1 classifies system as "internal testing utility rather than a market-facing product or service." Complete implementation in `server.js` (15 lines total) shows single request handler with static response. Section 3.4.1 confirms zero test framework dependencies in `package.json`. Section 5.1.1.1 documents "minimalist monolithic architecture" with "zero-dependency design."

**Architectural Factors Precluding Comprehensive Testing:**

| Factor | System Characteristic | Testing Implication |
|--------|---------------------|-------------------|
| **Code Complexity** | 15 lines, single function, no branches | Testing overhead exceeds implementation complexity |
| **Business Logic** | None - static string literal response | No algorithmic behavior to validate |
| **External Dependencies** | Zero (only Node.js http module) | No dependency mocking or integration testing needed |
| **Data Layer** | Stateless - no database, cache, or files | No data integrity, persistence, or consistency testing required |

**Operational Factors Precluding Comprehensive Testing:**

- **Purpose:** Test infrastructure for backprop integration validation (is itself the test target, not production code)
- **Deployment:** Localhost-only (127.0.0.1), developer workstation execution, manual start/stop
- **Users:** Single developer operator, no external customers, no multi-tenant concerns
- **Lifecycle:** Short-lived execution during testing sessions, immediate process termination acceptable
- **Risk Profile:** Zero business impact from failures, no revenue dependency, no user experience concerns

Section 5.1.1.1 describes "Zero-Dependency Design" and "Stateless Request Processing." `server.js` lines 6-10 show complete request handler with no conditional logic, loops, or data transformations. Section 2.4.1 lists "No Testing Infrastructure" as documented limitation.

### 6.6.2 Current Testing Approach (Manual Validation)

#### 6.6.2.1 Manual Smoke Testing Procedure

**Current Testing Methodology:**

The system relies exclusively on manual smoke testing performed by the developer during local development sessions. This lightweight approach provides immediate feedback without the overhead of automated test infrastructure.

**Testing Procedure (Actual Current Practice):**

```bash
# Step 1: Start Server
$ cd /path/to/hello_world_Oct_2025
$ node server.js
Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/

#### Step 2: Verify Server Response (New Terminal)
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:3000
Hello, World!

#### Step 3: Visual Verification
#### Expected: "Hello, World!" displayed in terminal
#### Actual: (developer visually confirms output matches expectation)

#### Step 4: Stop Server (Return to Server Terminal)
#### Press Ctrl+C (sends SIGINT signal)
#### Process terminates immediately

#### Test Result: ✅ PASS (if output matches "Hello, World!")
####             ❌ FAIL (if different output, error, or no response)
```

**Test Execution Flow:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Term1 as Terminal 1<br/>(Server)
    participant Term2 as Terminal 2<br/>(Client)
    participant Server as server.js<br/>Process
    participant OS as Operating System<br/>TCP/IP Stack
    
    Dev->>Term1: node server.js
    Term1->>Server: Start Process
    Server->>OS: Bind to 127.0.0.1:3000
    OS->>Server: Port Binding Successful
    Server->>Term1: console.log("Server running...")
    Term1->>Dev: Display Startup Message
    
    Note over Dev: Visual Check: Server Started ✅
    
    Dev->>Term2: curl http://127.0.0.1:3000
    Term2->>OS: HTTP GET Request
    OS->>Server: Forward to Port 3000
    Server->>Server: Generate Static Response
    Server->>OS: HTTP 200 + "Hello, World!"
    OS->>Term2: Return Response
    Term2->>Dev: Display Response Body
    
    Note over Dev: Visual Verification:<br/>Compare actual vs. expected output
    
    alt Output Matches "Hello, World!"
        Note over Dev: ✅ TEST PASSED
    else Output Different or Error
        Note over Dev: ❌ TEST FAILED<br/>Investigate Issue
    end
    
    Dev->>Term1: Ctrl+C (SIGINT)
    Term1->>Server: Send Termination Signal
    Server->>OS: Close Port 3000
    Server->>Term1: Process Exit
    
    Note over Dev: Manual Test Complete
```

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 4.2.2 documents request handling workflow. Section 6.5.2.1 shows minimal logging (single startup message). Manual operation procedures documented in Section 5.4.3.4 with bash command examples.

#### 6.6.2.3 Test Failure Scenarios and Recovery

**Common Failure Scenarios:**

| Failure Mode | Symptom | Root Cause | Recovery Procedure |
|-------------|---------|-----------|-------------------|
| **Port Already in Use** | `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` | Previous server instance still running | Kill process: `lsof -ti:3000 \| xargs kill` then restart |
| **No Response** | curl hangs or times out | Server not started or crashed | Check process: `ps aux \| grep node`, restart if needed |
| **Wrong Output** | Response differs from "Hello, World!" | Code modified or file corrupted | Restore from git: `git checkout server.js`, restart |
| **Module Not Found** | `Error: Cannot find module 'http'` | Node.js not installed or incorrect version | Install Node.js v15+ |

**Error Recovery Flow:**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    ERROR[Test Failure Detected] --> SYMPTOM{Identify<br/>Symptom}
    
    SYMPTOM -->|EADDRINUSE| PORT_CONFLICT[Port Conflict]
    SYMPTOM -->|Timeout| NO_RESPONSE[Server Not Responding]
    SYMPTOM -->|Wrong Output| WRONG_OUTPUT[Incorrect Response]
    SYMPTOM -->|Module Error| MISSING_DEP[Missing Node.js]
    
    PORT_CONFLICT --> KILL_PROCESS["Kill Conflicting Process<br/>lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill"]
    NO_RESPONSE --> CHECK_PROCESS{Server<br/>Process<br/>Running?}
    WRONG_OUTPUT --> CHECK_CODE[Compare server.js<br/>with Git Repository]
    MISSING_DEP --> INSTALL_NODE[Install Node.js v15+]
    
    KILL_PROCESS --> RESTART1[Restart Server]
    
    CHECK_PROCESS -->|Yes| CHECK_PORT{Port 3000<br/>Listening?}
    CHECK_PROCESS -->|No| RESTART2[Start Server]
    
    CHECK_PORT -->|No| RESTART2
    CHECK_PORT -->|Yes - Other Issue| INVESTIGATE[Investigate Firewall/<br/>Network Config]
    
    CHECK_CODE --> DIFF{Code<br/>Modified?}
    DIFF -->|Yes| RESTORE[git restore server.js]
    DIFF -->|No - Corrupted| CLONE[git clone repository]
    
    INSTALL_NODE --> VERIFY_VERSION[node --version]
    
    RESTART1 --> RETEST[Re-run Manual Tests]
    RESTART2 --> RETEST
    RESTORE --> RESTART3[Restart Server]
    RESTART3 --> RETEST
    CLONE --> RESTART3
    VERIFY_VERSION --> RETEST
    
    RETEST --> RESOLVED{Tests<br/>Pass?}
    RESOLVED -->|Yes| SUCCESS[✅ Issue Resolved]
    RESOLVED -->|No| INVESTIGATE
    INVESTIGATE --> EXTERNAL[Seek External Help<br/>Stack Overflow, GitHub Issues]
    
    style ERROR fill:#F44336
    style SUCCESS fill:#4CAF50
```

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.3.4 documents "Recovery Procedures: Manual Developer Intervention" with bash command examples for port conflict resolution and code restoration. Section 6.5.4.2 shows incident response flow for manual troubleshooting.

**Example Unit Test Implementation (Not Currently Implemented):**

```javascript
// test/server.test.js - EXAMPLE ONLY (does not exist in repository)

const http = require('http');

describe('Hello World Server', () => {
  let server;
  const port = 3001; // Use different port for testing
  
  beforeAll((done) => {
    // Start server before tests
    server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
      res.statusCode = 200;
      res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
      res.end('Hello, World!\n');
    });
    server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1', done);
  });
  
  afterAll((done) => {
    // Stop server after tests
    server.close(done);
  });
  
  test('should return 200 status code', (done) => {
    http.get(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}`, (res) => {
      expect(res.statusCode).toBe(200);
      done();
    });
  });
  
  test('should return "Hello, World!" response body', (done) => {
    http.get(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}`, (res) => {
      let data = '';
      res.on('data', chunk => data += chunk);
      res.on('end', () => {
        expect(data).toBe('Hello, World!\n');
        done();
      });
    });
  });
  
  test('should return Content-Type: text/plain header', (done) => {
    http.get(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}`, (res) => {
      expect(res.headers['content-type']).toBe('text/plain');
      done();
    });
  });
  
  test('should respond in less than 100ms', (done) => {
    const start = Date.now();
    http.get(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}`, (res) => {
      res.on('end', () => {
        const duration = Date.now() - start;
        expect(duration).toBeLessThan(100);
        done();
      });
    });
  });
});
```

### 6.6.8 Security Testing Considerations

#### 6.6.8.1 Security Testing Status: NOT APPLICABLE

**Security Testing Assessment:**

Security testing validates defense mechanisms against malicious attacks. This system has:

- **No authentication** to test (no credentials, tokens, or sessions)
- **No authorization** to validate (no access control or permissions)
- **No user input processing** (request data ignored, no injection vulnerabilities)
- **No data storage** (stateless, no data breaches possible)
- **Localhost-only deployment** (network isolation prevents external attacks)

### 6.6.11 Testing Strategy Diagrams

#### 6.6.11.1 Test Execution Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    START([Developer Ready to Test]) --> CHECK_SERVER{Server<br/>Running?}
    
    CHECK_SERVER -->|No| START_SERVER[node server.js]
    CHECK_SERVER -->|Yes - Port Conflict| KILL_PROCESS["Kill Existing Process<br/>lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill"]
    
    KILL_PROCESS --> START_SERVER
    START_SERVER --> WAIT_STARTUP["Wait for Startup Message<br/>Server running at..."]
    
    WAIT_STARTUP --> VERIFY_STARTUP{Startup<br/>Message<br/>Displayed?}
    
    VERIFY_STARTUP -->|No - Error| DIAGNOSE_ERROR[Diagnose Error<br/>Check error message]
    VERIFY_STARTUP -->|Yes| READY[Server Ready for Testing]
    
    READY --> TEST_1[Test 1: Send HTTP Request<br/>curl http://127.0.0.1:3000]
    TEST_1 --> CHECK_RESPONSE{Response<br/>Received?}
    
    CHECK_RESPONSE -->|No - Timeout| FAIL_TIMEOUT[❌ FAIL: No Response<br/>Check server process]
    CHECK_RESPONSE -->|Yes| VERIFY_BODY{Body =<br/>Hello, World!?}
    
    VERIFY_BODY -->|No| FAIL_BODY[❌ FAIL: Wrong Body<br/>Investigate code changes]
    VERIFY_BODY -->|Yes| TEST_2[Test 2: Verify Status Code<br/>curl -i localhost:3000]
    
    TEST_2 --> CHECK_STATUS{Status =<br/>200 OK?}
    
    CHECK_STATUS -->|No| FAIL_STATUS[❌ FAIL: Wrong Status<br/>Check response handling]
    CHECK_STATUS -->|Yes| TEST_3[Test 3: Verify Header<br/>Check Content-Type]
    
    TEST_3 --> CHECK_HEADER{Header =<br/>text/plain?}
    
    CHECK_HEADER -->|No| FAIL_HEADER[❌ FAIL: Wrong Header<br/>Check setHeader call]
    CHECK_HEADER -->|Yes| ALL_TESTS_PASS[✅ ALL TESTS PASSED]
    
    ALL_TESTS_PASS --> CONTINUE_WORK{Continue<br/>Development?}
    
    CONTINUE_WORK -->|Yes| KEEP_RUNNING[Keep Server Running]
    CONTINUE_WORK -->|No| STOP_SERVER[Stop Server<br/>Ctrl+C]
    
    KEEP_RUNNING --> MAKE_CHANGES[Make Code Changes]
    MAKE_CHANGES --> RESTART[Restart Server]
    RESTART --> READY
    
    STOP_SERVER --> END([Testing Complete])
    
    DIAGNOSE_ERROR --> FIX_ERROR[Fix Error]
    FIX_ERROR --> START_SERVER
    
    FAIL_TIMEOUT --> FIX_ERROR
    FAIL_BODY --> FIX_ERROR
    FAIL_STATUS --> FIX_ERROR
    FAIL_HEADER --> FIX_ERROR
    
    style START fill:#2196F3
    style ALL_TESTS_PASS fill:#4CAF50
    style FAIL_TIMEOUT fill:#F44336
    style FAIL_BODY fill:#F44336
    style FAIL_STATUS fill:#F44336
    style FAIL_HEADER fill:#F44336
    style END fill:#2196F3
```

## 6.1 Core Services Architecture

### 6.1.1 Applicability Assessment

#### 6.1.1.1 Core Services Architecture Classification

**DEFINITIVE STATEMENT: Core Services Architecture is NOT APPLICABLE for this system.**

The hao-backprop-test repository implements a minimal, single-file, monolithic Node.js HTTP server designed exclusively for local integration testing purposes. This system fundamentally lacks the distributed architecture characteristics that would necessitate a Core Services Architecture design.

**Architecture Classification:**
- **Type**: Single-file monolithic test infrastructure
- **Deployment Model**: Localhost-only (127.0.0.1:3000)
- **Service Count**: 1 (indivisible monolithic component)
- **Distribution**: None (cannot distribute due to localhost binding)
- **Scaling Model**: Not applicable (single instance only)

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 5.1.1.1 classifies the architecture as "Single-file monolithic test infrastructure." Complete implementation contained in `server.js` (15 lines total). Section 5.1.1.3 explicitly states "No Service Boundaries: Not a microservices architecture; all functionality in one component."

#### 6.1.1.2 Rationale for Non-Applicability

Core Services Architecture addresses the challenges of distributed systems through service decomposition, inter-service communication patterns, and resilience mechanisms. This system deliberately rejects distributed architecture in favor of radical simplicity:

| Distributed Architecture Characteristic | Industry Standard | This System | Justification |
|----------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------|---------------|
| **Service Boundaries** | Multiple services with distinct responsibilities | Single component | All functionality in one 15-line file |
| **Inter-Service Communication** | REST APIs, message queues, gRPC | Not applicable | No services to communicate |
| **Service Discovery** | Consul, Eureka, etcd | Not implemented | Hard-coded hostname and port |
| **Load Distribution** | Load balancers, service mesh | Not implemented | Localhost binding prevents distribution |

**Primary Design Constraint**: The server binds exclusively to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), creating an operating system-enforced boundary that prevents external network access and distributed deployment patterns. This architectural decision eliminates the need for service architecture patterns while providing security through network isolation.

**Evidence**: Localhost binding implemented at `server.js` line 3: `const hostname = '127.0.0.1';`. Technical Specification Section 1.2.1.2 documents "Localhost-Only Access: Server binds exclusively to 127.0.0.1, preventing external network access."

#### 6.1.1.3 System Purpose and Scope

The system serves as integration testing infrastructure rather than a production service:

**Intended Use Cases:**
- Backprop integration testing (as stated in `README.md`)
- Local development validation
- HTTP server behavior verification
- Integration test target endpoint

**Explicitly Out of Scope:**
- Production deployment
- External user access
- Distributed service architecture
- High availability requirements
- Scalability beyond single developer usage

**Evidence**: `README.md` states: "This is a test project for backprop integration." Technical Specification Section 1.2.1.1 positions system as "internal testing utility rather than a market-facing product or service."

### 6.1.2 Monolithic Architecture Analysis

#### 6.1.2.1 System Architecture Overview

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Developer Workstation (127.0.0.1)"
        subgraph "Node.js Process (Single Instance)"
            SERVER[server.js<br/>15-line HTTP Server<br/>Monolithic Component]
            HTTP[Node.js http Module<br/>Built-in Library]
            
            SERVER -->|requires| HTTP
        end
        
        EVENTLOOP[Event Loop<br/>Single-threaded JS Execution]
        SOCKET[TCP Socket<br/>127.0.0.1:3000]
        
        HTTP --> EVENTLOOP
        HTTP --> SOCKET
        
        CLIENT[Local Test Client<br/>curl, browser, test script]
        CLIENT -->|HTTP Request| SOCKET
        SOCKET -->|HTTP 200 + Hello World| CLIENT
    end
    
    EXTERNAL[External Network]
    EXTERNAL -.->|Blocked by OS| SOCKET
    
    style SERVER fill:#4CAF50
    style SOCKET fill:#2196F3
    style EXTERNAL fill:#F44336
    style EVENTLOOP fill:#FF9800
```

**Architectural Characteristics:**

1. **Single Component**: Entire application contained in one JavaScript file (`server.js`)
2. **Zero Dependencies**: Uses only Node.js built-in `http` module
3. **Network Isolation**: Operating system routing prevents external access
4. **Stateless Processing**: No data persistence or session management
5. **Synchronous Callbacks**: Request handlers execute with predictable control flow

**Evidence**: Complete system implementation visible in `server.js` lines 1-15. Technical Specification Section 5.1.2 documents component architecture with dependency diagram showing single application layer component.

#### 6.1.2.2 Component Boundaries (Absence Thereof)

**No Internal Service Boundaries:**

The system implements zero separation of concerns, with all functionality co-located:

- **No Routing Layer**: All HTTP paths handled identically
- **No Business Logic Layer**: No data processing or computation
- **No Data Access Layer**: No database or persistence mechanisms
- **No Integration Layer**: No external service calls
- **No Presentation Layer**: Static text response without templating

**Monolithic Request Processing Flow:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as HTTP Client
    participant OS as Operating System
    participant E as Event Loop
    participant H as Request Handler
    participant R as Response Generator
    
    C->>OS: TCP SYN (connect to 127.0.0.1:3000)
    OS->>E: Accept Connection
    C->>E: HTTP Request (any method/path)
    E->>H: Invoke Callback (req, res)
    Note over H: req parameter ignored<br/>No processing
    H->>R: Static Response Generation
    R->>R: statusCode = 200
    R->>R: setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')
    R->>R: body = 'Hello, World!\n'
    R->>E: end() - Finalize Response
    E->>C: HTTP 200 + Hello, World!
    E->>OS: Close TCP Connection
```

**Processing Characteristics:**
- **Latency**: <5ms (no I/O operations)
- **Memory**: <1KB per request (transient objects only)
- **CPU**: Negligible (static string copy operation)

**Evidence**: Request handler implementation at `server.js` lines 6-10 shows no layering or modularization. Technical Specification Section 5.1.1.3 states "Monolithic with no component separation."

#### 6.1.3.5 Circuit Breaker Patterns

**Status**: NOT IMPLEMENTED - No failure protection mechanisms

**Analysis**: Circuit breaker patterns (Hystrix, Resilience4j, Polly) protect distributed systems from cascading failures by detecting faults and preventing repeated calls to failing services. This system has no external calls to protect:

**Circuit Breaker Applicability:**

| Failure Scenario | Circuit Breaker Response | This System |
|-----------------|-------------------------|-------------|
| **Downstream Service Timeout** | Open circuit, fail fast | No downstream services |
| **Downstream Service Error Rate** | Trip breaker after threshold | No external calls |
| **Dependency Unavailable** | Return fallback response | No dependencies to fail |
| **Network Partition** | Degrade gracefully | Localhost (no network) |

**Error Handling Reality:**

```javascript
// server.js lines 6-10: No error handling
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  // ❌ No try-catch
  // ❌ No error detection
  // ❌ No circuit breaker
  // ❌ No fallback logic
  
  res.statusCode = 200;
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
  res.end('Hello, World!\n');
});

// Any exception = immediate process crash
```

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 5.4.3.1 states "Critical Finding: The system implements zero error handling mechanisms." Complete code review confirms no try-catch blocks, no error listeners, no resilience patterns.

#### 6.1.3.6 Retry and Fallback Mechanisms

**Status**: NOT IMPLEMENTED - No retry logic or fallbacks

**Analysis**: Retry mechanisms (exponential backoff, idempotent request retry) and fallback strategies handle transient failures in distributed systems. This system performs no operations that could fail transiently:

**Retry Pattern Assessment:**

- **Outbound HTTP Requests**: None (no API calls to retry)
- **Database Queries**: None (no database to query)
- **Message Queue Operations**: None (no queue)
- **File System I/O**: None (no file writes)
- **External Service Calls**: None (no integrations)

**Fallback Strategy Assessment:**

- **Primary Response**: Static "Hello, World!" literal (cannot fail)
- **Fallback Response**: Not needed (primary always succeeds)
- **Cache Fallback**: Not applicable (no cache)
- **Default Values**: Not applicable (no data retrieval)

**Why Retry Not Needed**: Static response generation requires only CPU (string literal copy). Operation is deterministic and cannot fail due to transient conditions.

**Evidence**: Request handler at `server.js` lines 7-9 performs only memory operations (set status code, set header, write static string). Technical Specification Section 5.1.4.1 confirms "Zero external service dependencies."

**Horizontal Scaling Barriers:**

1. **Localhost Binding**: Cannot deploy to multiple machines (127.0.0.1 not routable)
2. **Port Conflict**: Cannot run multiple instances on same machine (port 3000 hard-coded)
3. **No Load Balancer**: No traffic distribution mechanism
4. **No Session Affinity**: Not needed (stateless), but no infrastructure for it

**Vertical Scaling Analysis:**

Vertical scaling (adding CPU/RAM to single machine) provides **minimal benefit**:

| Resource | Current Usage | Maximum Usage | Scaling Benefit |
|----------|---------------|---------------|-----------------|
| **CPU** | ~2-3% idle | ~10% at 1000 req/sec | Ceiling: Single-threaded JavaScript |
| **Memory** | ~20-50MB | ~100MB at high load | Static response uses minimal memory |
| **Network** | Minimal | Loopback (infinite bandwidth) | Already optimal (no network I/O) |
| **Disk I/O** | Zero | Zero | No disk operations |

**Conclusion**: System bottlenecked by single-threaded event loop (~1000 req/sec), not by CPU/RAM. Vertical scaling cannot improve beyond this architectural limit.

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 3.7.3 states "Localhost binding prevents distributed deployment" and "No containerization implemented." Performance ceiling documented in Section 5.4.5.2 as "~1000 req/sec throughput ceiling."

#### 6.1.4.4 Performance Optimization Techniques

**Status**: NOT IMPLEMENTED - Optimization not needed

**Performance Philosophy**: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil" - current performance exceeds requirements by orders of magnitude, rendering optimization counterproductive.

**Optimization Assessment:**

| Optimization Technique | Performance Gain | Complexity Cost | Implementation Decision |
|-----------------------|-----------------|----------------|------------------------|
| **Response Caching** | Negative impact | Low | ❌ Static literal faster than cache lookup |
| **Connection Pooling** | 5-10% improvement | Medium | ❌ Not needed (< 10ms already) |
| **HTTP/2 Protocol** | 10-20% improvement | Medium | ❌ Requires different module |
| **Compression (gzip)** | Minimal (14-byte response) | Low | ❌ Overhead > benefit |
| **Worker Threads** | 2-4x throughput | High | ❌ Requires state sharing complexity |
| **Clustering** | 2-4x throughput | Medium | ❌ Test infrastructure doesn't justify |
| **Keep-Alive Connections** | 10-15% improvement | Low | ❌ Implicit in HTTP/1.1 |

**Current Performance vs. Requirements:**

```
Performance Metrics:
├─ Response Latency: 1-5ms (Target: <10ms) ✅ 2-10x better than target
├─ Throughput: 500-1000 req/sec (Target: 100 req/sec) ✅ 5-10x better than target
├─ Memory Usage: 20-50MB (Target: <100MB) ✅ 2-5x better than target
└─ CPU Usage: 2-3% idle (Target: <5%) ✅ Within target
```

**Why No Optimization Implemented**: Test infrastructure workload is <100 req/day during manual testing. Current capacity of 500-1000 req/sec represents 43,200,000 - 86,400,000 req/day theoretical maximum. Optimization would provide zero practical benefit while increasing code complexity.

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 5.4.5.4 states "Current performance (1-5ms response, 500-1000 req/sec throughput) exceeds testing requirements by orders of magnitude." Performance analysis in Section 2.4.2 confirms sub-10ms latency target exceeded.

### 6.1.5 Resilience Patterns

#### 6.1.5.1 Fault Tolerance Mechanisms

**Status**: NOT IMPLEMENTED - Zero fault tolerance

**Fault Tolerance Analysis:**

Fault tolerance (system continues operating despite component failures) requires redundancy and error recovery mechanisms. This system implements neither:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Fault Tolerance Architecture (NOT IMPLEMENTED)"
        PRIMARY[Primary Instance]
        BACKUP[Backup Instance]
        HEALTH[Health Monitoring]
        
        HEALTH -->|Detects Failure| PRIMARY
        HEALTH -->|Triggers Failover| BACKUP
        BACKUP -.->|Takes Over| PRIMARY
    end
    
    subgraph "Actual Implementation"
        SINGLE[Single Instance<br/>No Redundancy]
        ERROR[Any Error]
        CRASH[Process Crash<br/>Complete Failure]
        
        ERROR --> CRASH
        SINGLE --> ERROR
    end
    
    MANUAL[Manual Recovery<br/>Developer restarts process]
    CRASH --> MANUAL
    
    style PRIMARY fill:#ccc
    style BACKUP fill:#ccc
    style HEALTH fill:#ccc
    style SINGLE fill:#2196F3
    style CRASH fill:#F44336
    style MANUAL fill:#FF9800
```

**Fault Tolerance Mechanisms Assessment:**

| Mechanism | Purpose | Implementation Status | Impact of Absence |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|-------------------|
| **Redundant Instances** | Survive single instance failure | ❌ Not implemented | Any failure = complete outage |
| **Error Handling** | Catch and recover from errors | ❌ Not implemented | Any exception = process crash |
| **Health Checks** | Detect unhealthy instances | ❌ Not implemented | Failures undetected until crash |
| **Graceful Degradation** | Reduce functionality vs. failing completely | ❌ Not implemented | Binary state: working or crashed |
| **Bulkhead Pattern** | Isolate failures to subsystems | ❌ Not applicable | Single component (no subsystems) |

**Failure Modes and Effects:**

```
Failure Scenario: Uncaught Exception in Request Handler
├─ Detection: Immediate (process terminates)
├─ Notification: None (no alerting)
├─ Failover: None (no backup instance)
├─ Recovery: Manual restart by developer
├─ Downtime: Until developer notices and restarts (~1-5 minutes)
└─ Data Loss: None (stateless architecture)
```

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 5.4.3.1 states "Critical Finding: The system implements zero error handling mechanisms." Section 5.4.3.2 documents all error types result in "immediate process crash."

#### 6.1.5.2 Disaster Recovery Procedures

**Status**: MANUAL PROCEDURES ONLY - No automated DR

**Disaster Recovery Strategy:**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    DISASTER[Disaster Event] --> DETECT{Developer<br/>Detection}
    
    DETECT -->|Process Crashed| SCENARIO1[Scenario 1:<br/>Process Crash]
    DETECT -->|Port Conflict| SCENARIO2[Scenario 2:<br/>Port Unavailable]
    DETECT -->|Code Corruption| SCENARIO3[Scenario 3:<br/>Code Error]
    DETECT -->|Machine Failure| SCENARIO4[Scenario 4:<br/>Hardware Failure]
    
    SCENARIO1 --> RESTART1[Terminal: node server.js]
    SCENARIO2 --> KILL[Kill Conflicting Process]
    SCENARIO3 --> GIT[Restore from Git]
    SCENARIO4 --> REBOOT[Reboot Machine]
    
    KILL --> RESTART1
    GIT --> RESTART1
    REBOOT --> RESTART1
    
    RESTART1 --> VERIFY{Verification}
    VERIFY -->|Success| OPERATIONAL[✅ Service Operational]
    VERIFY -->|Failure| ESCALATE[Manual Troubleshooting]
    
    style DISASTER fill:#F44336
    style OPERATIONAL fill:#4CAF50
    style RESTART1 fill:#2196F3
```

**Disaster Recovery Metrics:**

| Metric | Definition | This System |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** | Maximum acceptable downtime | <1 minute (manual restart) |
| **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** | Maximum acceptable data loss | N/A (stateless, no data) |
| **MTTR (Mean Time To Repair)** | Average time to restore service | 1-5 minutes (depends on failure type) |
| **MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)** | Average operating time between failures | Not tracked (no monitoring) |

**Recovery Procedures by Disaster Type:**

**1. Process Crash Recovery:**
```bash
# RTO: <1 minute
# Detection: Terminal shows process exit
# Recovery:
$ node server.js
# Verification:
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:3000
# Expected: "Hello, World!"
```

**2. Port Conflict Recovery:**
```bash
# RTO: 1-2 minutes
# Detection: EADDRINUSE error on startup
# Recovery:
$ lsof -i :3000  # Identify conflicting process
$ kill <PID>     # Terminate conflicting process
$ node server.js # Restart server
# Verification:
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:3000
```

**3. Code Corruption Recovery:**
```bash
# RTO: 2-5 minutes
# Detection: Syntax errors, runtime exceptions
# Recovery:
$ git status           # Check for local changes
$ git restore server.js  # Restore from Git
# OR
$ git clone https://github.com/lakshya-blitzy/hello_world_Oct_2025.git
$ cd hello_world_Oct_2025
$ node server.js
# Verification:
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:3000
```

**4. Machine Failure Recovery:**
```bash
# RTO: 5-10 minutes
# Detection: Machine unresponsive
# Recovery:
# 1. Reboot machine (OS-specific procedure)
# 2. Navigate to project directory
$ cd path/to/hello_world_Oct_2025
$ node server.js
# Verification:
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:3000
```

**Evidence**: Disaster recovery procedures documented in Technical Specification Section 5.4.6.1. Manual recovery approach justified in Section 5.4.6.2 due to test infrastructure scope. Git backup strategy implicit in repository workflow.

### 6.1.6 Architectural Constraints and Trade-offs

#### 6.1.6.1 Design Constraints

**Fundamental Architectural Constraints:**

| Constraint Type | Constraint Description | Impact on Service Architecture |
|----------------|------------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Network Isolation** | Localhost-only binding (127.0.0.1) | Prevents distributed deployment, eliminates service mesh patterns |
| **Single File Limit** | All code in 15-line file | No modular service decomposition possible |
| **Zero Dependencies** | Only Node.js built-in modules | Cannot use service discovery, circuit breaker libraries |
| **Test Infrastructure Scope** | Not production system | No business justification for production patterns |
| **Hard-Coded Configuration** | Port and hostname in source | Cannot run multiple instances, dynamic scaling impossible |

**Constraint Propagation:**

```
Localhost Binding (127.0.0.1)
  ↓
Cannot access from other machines
  ↓
Cannot distribute across servers
  ↓
Cannot implement load balancing
  ↓
Cannot achieve horizontal scaling
  ↓
Cannot implement high availability
  ↓
Core Services Architecture Not Applicable
```

**Evidence**: Localhost binding constraint at `server.js` line 3. Technical Specification Section 4.3.1.1 documents "Operating system routing table prevents external traffic from reaching loopback-bound services."

#### 6.1.6.2 Architectural Trade-offs

**Simplicity vs. Resilience Trade-off:**

The architecture deliberately prioritizes simplicity over resilience for integration testing use case:

**Chosen: Simplicity**
- ✅ 15 lines of code (total)
- ✅ Zero dependencies to manage
- ✅ No configuration complexity
- ✅ Instant comprehension by developers
- ✅ No deployment infrastructure
- ✅ No operational overhead

**Rejected: Resilience**
- ❌ No error handling (any exception crashes process)
- ❌ No health checks (failures undetected)
- ❌ No redundancy (single point of failure)
- ❌ No auto-recovery (manual restart required)
- ❌ No monitoring (no visibility)

**Justification**: Test infrastructure operated manually by developer who is present to observe and recover from failures. Resilience mechanisms would add complexity without proportional benefit.

**Performance vs. Features Trade-off:**

**Chosen: Performance**
- ✅ Sub-5ms response latency
- ✅ Static response (no processing overhead)
- ✅ Minimal memory footprint (<50MB)

**Rejected: Features**
- ❌ No routing (all paths identical)
- ❌ No request parsing (input ignored)
- ❌ No dynamic content (static literal only)

**Justification**: Integration testing requires predictable, fast responses. Feature richness would introduce variability and complexity without testing value.

**Evidence**: Trade-off analysis in Technical Specification Section 3.1. Architectural principles documented in Section 5.1.1.2 emphasizing "Minimalism Over Features" and "Predictability Over Flexibility."

## 6.2 Database Design

### 6.2.1 Applicability Assessment

**Database Design is not applicable to this system.**

The hao-backprop-test repository implements a completely stateless HTTP server with zero persistence mechanisms. The system contains no database systems, no data storage layers, and no caching infrastructure. This architectural decision is intentional and aligned with the system's purpose as lightweight test infrastructure.

#### 6.2.1.1 System Architecture Analysis

The system architecture exhibits the following characteristics that eliminate the need for database design:

**Stateless Request Processing**: Every HTTP request is processed independently with no state retention between requests. The request handler in `server.js` ignores all incoming request data and returns a static string literal (`"Hello, World!\n"`) for every request regardless of HTTP method, path, or payload.

**Zero Persistence Requirements**: The system generates static responses using hard-coded string literals embedded directly in the source code. No user data, session information, application state, configuration data, or operational logs require persistent storage. All data exists ephemerally during the request-response cycle only.

**Single-File Implementation**: The entire HTTP server implementation consists of 15 lines of code in `server.js` that import only Node.js built-in modules (`http`). The codebase contains no database connection code, no data access layers, no ORM configurations, and no schema definitions.

#### 6.2.1.2 Dependency Analysis

Analysis of `package.json` confirms the complete absence of database-related dependencies:

**No Database Drivers**: The manifest contains zero dependencies and zero devDependencies. Common database client libraries are explicitly absent, including:
- Relational database drivers (pg, mysql, mysql2, sqlite3)
- Document database clients (mongodb, mongoose)
- Key-value store clients (redis, ioredis)
- ORM frameworks (sequelize, typeorm, prisma)
- Database connection pooling libraries

**No Storage Services**: The system integrates with no external storage services including object storage (AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage), file storage systems, or cloud database services.

#### 6.2.1.3 Codebase Structure Verification

The repository structure confirms the absence of database-related components:

**Missing Database Directories**: The root folder contains only 4 files (README.md, package.json, package-lock.json, server.js) with zero subdirectories. Database-supporting directories are absent:
- No `/models` directory for data models
- No `/schemas` directory for schema definitions
- No `/migrations` directory for database migrations
- No `/database` or `/db` directory for database configuration
- No `/config` directory for connection strings or credentials

**No Configuration Files**: The codebase contains no environment configuration files (.env), no database connection configuration, and no credential management files.

### 6.2.2 Architectural Rationale

#### 6.2.2.1 Stateless Design Principles

The system implements a stateless architecture by design, which fundamentally eliminates the need for persistent storage:

**Request Independence**: Each HTTP request is processed in complete isolation. The request handler function executes identically for every invocation, with no access to shared state, session data, or historical information. Process restarts have zero data loss because no data is stored.

**Predictable Behavior**: The test infrastructure prioritizes predictability and reproducibility. Static response generation ensures consistent behavior across all invocations, eliminating variability introduced by database queries, cache states, or persisted configuration.

**Minimal Dependencies**: The zero-dependency architecture reduces complexity, eliminates external failure points, and simplifies deployment. Database systems would introduce unnecessary operational overhead for a system that generates static responses.

#### 6.2.2.2 Test Infrastructure Purpose

The system's role as test infrastructure for backpropagation integration testing informs the architectural decisions:

**Localhost-Only Operation**: The server binds exclusively to 127.0.0.1:3000, serving only local development requests. Single-developer manual operation eliminates multi-user data management requirements, concurrent access control needs, and distributed data consistency concerns.

**Manual Operation**: The system is executed manually by a single developer for integration testing purposes. No automated production deployment, no 24/7 availability requirements, and no service-level agreements exist that would necessitate backup systems or fault-tolerant data storage.

**Performance Characteristics**: Static response generation achieves sub-millisecond latency (1-5ms actual vs. <10ms target), exceeding performance requirements by 10x. Database queries would introduce unnecessary latency for a system that generates responses from string literals.

**No Data Backup**: No data backup infrastructure exists because no data requires backup. Stateless architecture eliminates data loss risk during process restarts or system failures.

## 6.3 Integration Architecture

### 6.3.1 Applicability Assessment

**Integration Architecture is not applicable to this system.**

The hao-backprop-test repository implements a minimal, single-file HTTP server designed exclusively as test infrastructure for local development. This system fundamentally lacks the characteristics that would necessitate integration architecture design: it has zero external system connections, no API gateway configuration, no message processing infrastructure, and no third-party service dependencies beyond Git version control.

#### 6.3.1.1 Architectural Classification

**System Type**: Stateless Test Endpoint
- **Purpose**: Local integration testing target ("test project for backprop integration")
- **Deployment Model**: Localhost-only (127.0.0.1:3000)
- **External Integrations**: None (zero dependencies in `package.json`)
- **Integration Role**: Test target to be integrated with, not an integration platform

**Evidence**: The `README.md` explicitly states the system is a "test project for backprop integration." Analysis of `package.json` confirms zero dependencies or devDependencies sections, indicating no external library integrations. The `server.js` file (15 lines total) imports only the Node.js built-in `http` module with no external API calls, database connections, or message queue integrations.

Comprehensive analysis of the codebase and technical specification confirms the complete absence of integration architecture components:

|---------------------|------------------------------|-------------|-----------------|

| **External APIs** | REST clients, GraphQL, gRPC | ❌ Not implemented | No HTTP client libraries in dependencies |

**Only External Integration**: GitHub repository hosting at `https://github.com/lakshya-blitzy/hello_world_Oct_2025` used exclusively for version control and source code storage, not runtime integration.

#### 6.3.1.3 Rationale for Non-Applicability

The system's architectural design intentionally excludes integration architecture patterns for the following reasons:

**1. Test Infrastructure Scope**

The system serves as internal testing infrastructure operated manually by a single developer. Integration architecture patterns (service mesh, circuit breakers, retry logic) address production concerns like distributed system resilience, high availability, and scalability that are not applicable to local test endpoints.

**2. Localhost Network Isolation**

The server binds exclusively to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), creating an operating system-enforced network boundary that prevents external connections. This architectural constraint eliminates distributed integration patterns including:
- Cross-network API calls (no external systems can reach localhost)
- Load balancing (cannot distribute across machines)
- Service discovery (hard-coded hostname and port)
- Multi-region deployment (single machine only)

**Evidence**: `server.js` line 3 hard-codes `const hostname = '127.0.0.1';`, binding the server to localhost. Technical Specification Section 4.3.1.1 documents that operating system routing tables prevent external traffic from reaching loopback-bound services.

**3. Stateless Architecture**

The system maintains zero persistent state between requests. All processing consists of returning a static string literal ("Hello, World!\n") without accessing databases, caches, or external services. Stateless design eliminates the need for:
- Data synchronization across services
- State replication mechanisms
- Cache invalidation strategies
- Transaction coordination

**Evidence**: The request handler in `server.js` lines 6-10 ignores the request parameter entirely and returns a hard-coded response for every invocation. Technical Specification Section 6.2.1 confirms "completely stateless HTTP server with zero persistence mechanisms."

**4. Zero-Dependency Philosophy**

The deliberate decision to use only Node.js built-in modules eliminates all external integration points. No npm packages means no third-party API clients, no database drivers, no messaging libraries, and no external service SDKs.

**Evidence**: `package.json` contains no `dependencies` or `devDependencies` sections. The only import statement in `server.js` line 1 is `const http = require('http');`, which references Node.js's built-in HTTP module.

#### 6.3.3.2 Request Processing Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as HTTP Client
    participant OS as Operating System<br/>TCP/IP Stack
    participant NodeJS as Node.js<br/>Event Loop
    participant Handler as Request Handler<br/>(server.js)
    
    Client->>OS: TCP SYN<br/>(Connect to 127.0.0.1:3000)
    OS->>NodeJS: Accept Connection
    Client->>NodeJS: HTTP Request<br/>(Method, Path, Headers, Body)
    
    NodeJS->>Handler: Invoke Callback<br/>(req, res)
    
    Note over Handler: ❌ req parameter ignored<br/>❌ No routing logic<br/>❌ No validation<br/>❌ No business logic
    
    Handler->>Handler: Set statusCode = 200
    Handler->>Handler: Set Content-Type header
    Handler->>Handler: Write body: "Hello, World!\n"
    
    Handler->>NodeJS: res.end()
    NodeJS->>Client: HTTP Response<br/>200 OK + Body
    NodeJS->>OS: Close TCP Connection
    
    Note over Client,Handler: Total Processing Time: 1-5ms<br/>(Static response, no I/O)
```

**Processing Characteristics**:

**Request Phase**:
- Client establishes TCP connection to 127.0.0.1:3000
- HTTP request transmitted (any method, any path, any headers)
- Node.js http module parses request into `req` object
- Request object immediately ignored by handler

**Response Phase**:
- Response status code set to 200 (hard-coded)
- Content-Type header set to "text/plain" (hard-coded)
- Response body set to "Hello, World!\n" (string literal)
- Response stream finalized with `res.end()`

**Performance Characteristics**:
- **Latency**: 1-5ms actual (vs. <10ms target)
- **Throughput**: 500-1000 requests/second capacity
- **Memory**: <1KB per request (transient objects)
- **CPU**: Negligible (string reference operation)

**Evidence**: Complete request handler implementation visible in `server.js` lines 6-10. Technical Specification Section 5.4.5 documents performance characteristics showing sub-10ms latency and 500-1000 req/sec throughput.

| Component | Value | Purpose |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| **Status Code** | 200 OK | Indicates successful request processing |
| **Status Line** | HTTP/1.1 200 OK | Protocol version + status |
| **Header: Content-Type** | text/plain | Indicates plain text response body |
| **Body** | Hello, World!\n | Static response content (14 bytes) |
| **Body Encoding** | UTF-8 | Default Node.js string encoding |

**Response Consistency**:

All requests receive identical responses regardless of:
- HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS, HEAD, TRACE)
- URL path (/, /api, /test, /nonexistent)
- Request headers (Authorization, Accept, User-Agent, etc.)
- Request body (JSON, XML, form data, binary)
- Query parameters (?param=value)

**Example Response**:
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
Date: Mon, 16 Oct 2025 12:00:00 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Content-Length: 14

Hello, World!

```

**Evidence**: Response generation in `server.js` lines 7-9 shows hard-coded status code (200), header (Content-Type: text/plain), and body ("Hello, World!\n"). No conditional logic exists that would vary the response based on request properties.

**Constraint Analysis**:

**1. Network Constraint**: Localhost binding (127.0.0.1) enforced at line 3 of `server.js` prevents:
   - Cross-machine communication (loopback not routable)
   - Distributed deployment (all instances must be same machine)
   - External system integration (no network path from outside)
   - Cloud deployment (cannot bind to public IP without code change)

**2. Port Conflict Constraint**: Hard-coded port 3000 at line 4 of `server.js` prevents:
   - Multiple instances on same machine (EADDRINUSE error)
   - Dynamic port allocation (required for container orchestration)
   - Port-based service versioning (/v1 on 3000, /v2 on 3001)

**3. Dependency Constraint**: Zero npm dependencies eliminates:
   - Integration libraries (no axios for HTTP clients, no redis for caching)
   - Circuit breaker implementations (no resilience libraries)
   - Message queue clients (no AMQP, Kafka, or AWS SDK)
   - Authentication providers (no passport, oauth libraries)

**4. Architectural Complexity Constraint**: 15-line single-file design prevents:
   - Service boundaries (no modular decomposition)
   - Layered architecture (no separation of concerns)
   - Dependency injection (no IoC containers)
   - Interface-based abstraction (direct implementation only)

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 6.1.6.1 documents "Fundamental Architectural Constraints" showing how localhost binding propagates through architecture to eliminate distributed patterns. Constraint propagation chain documented showing "Cannot access from other machines → Cannot distribute across servers → Cannot implement load balancing → Cannot achieve horizontal scaling → Core Services Architecture Not Applicable."

### 6.3.6 Alternative: Local Client Integration Patterns

#### 6.3.6.1 Supported Integration Scenarios

While the system implements no integration architecture, it does support integration testing scenarios through local client connections:

**Scenario 1: Manual Integration Testing**

```bash
# Command-line integration test
curl http://127.0.0.1:3000

#### Expected Output:
#### Hello, World!

#### Verify response status
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000

#### Expected Output:
## HTTP/1.1 200 OK
#### Content-Type: text/plain
##### ...
#### Hello, World!
```

**Scenario 2: Automated Test Script Integration**

```javascript
// Node.js integration test example
const http = require('http');

function testIntegration() {
  const options = {
    hostname: '127.0.0.1',
    port: 3000,
    path: '/',
    method: 'GET'
  };

  const req = http.request(options, (res) => {
    let data = '';
    
    res.on('data', (chunk) => {
      data += chunk;
    });
    
    res.on('end', () => {
      // Validate integration
      if (res.statusCode === 200 && data === 'Hello, World!\n') {
        console.log('✅ Integration test passed');
      } else {
        console.log('❌ Integration test failed');
      }
    });
  });

  req.on('error', (error) => {
    console.error('❌ Integration error:', error);
  });

  req.end();
}

testIntegration();
```

**Scenario 3: Testing Framework Integration**

```javascript
// Jest test suite example (not implemented in codebase)
const http = require('http');

describe('hao-backprop-test Integration', () => {
  test('should return Hello World response', (done) => {
    http.get('http://127.0.0.1:3000', (res) => {
      let data = '';
      
      res.on('data', (chunk) => data += chunk);
      res.on('end', () => {
        expect(res.statusCode).toBe(200);
        expect(res.headers['content-type']).toBe('text/plain');
        expect(data).toBe('Hello, World!\n');
        done();
      });
    });
  });
});
```

**Evidence**: Technical Specification Section 4.5.2 documents supported client integration methods including curl commands, web browsers, and test scripts. The examples above demonstrate how external systems would integrate with the test endpoint for validation purposes.

### 6.3.8 Summary

#### 6.3.8.1 Integration Architecture Status

**Current State**: Integration Architecture is definitively not applicable to this system. The hao-backprop-test repository implements a minimal, stateless, localhost-bound HTTP server with zero external integrations, no message processing infrastructure, no API design patterns, and no third-party service dependencies.

**Design Philosophy**: The system deliberately rejects integration architecture complexity in favor of radical simplicity appropriate for test infrastructure. The 15-line implementation achieves 100% of required functionality (predictable test endpoint) without the operational overhead of integration patterns designed for distributed production systems.

**Integration Role**: Rather than integrating with external systems, this system serves as an integration test target—a predictable endpoint that external systems can integrate with for validation purposes.

## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Security Architecture Overview

#### 6.4.1.1 Security Applicability Statement

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.** The hao-backprop-test project implements a minimal test server with no application-level security mechanisms. This is an intentional architectural decision aligned with the system's scope as local development test infrastructure rather than an oversight or security gap.

The system relies exclusively on **operating system-level network isolation** as its sole security control, implemented through localhost binding (127.0.0.1). This approach is appropriate for the system's classification as test-only infrastructure deployed exclusively on developer workstations during integration testing activities.

#### 6.4.1.2 Security Architecture Summary

**Security Control Classification:**

|---------------|---------------------|--------|-----------|

| Network Layer | Localhost binding | ✅ Implemented | OS-level isolation sufficient |
| Data Layer | None | ❌ Not Applicable | Stateless (no data storage) |

#### 6.4.1.3 Security Philosophy and Design Rationale

The security architecture embodies a **minimalist security model** appropriate for test infrastructure with the following design principles:

**Principle 1: Scope-Appropriate Security**
- Test infrastructure deployed exclusively on trusted developer workstations
- No production deployment, external access, or sensitive data handling
- Security controls proportional to risk profile and system classification

**Principle 2: OS-Level Trust Boundary**
- Operating system network stack enforces impenetrable boundary at kernel level
- Network protocols (RFC 1122) ensure loopback traffic never traverses physical interfaces
- Eliminates need for redundant application-level access controls

**Principle 3: Accepted Risk Model**
- Local machine compromise implies broader security failure
- Application-level authentication provides minimal additional protection if OS compromised
- Cost-benefit analysis favors simplicity over defense-in-depth for test scenarios

**Evidence:** Security decision rationale documented in Technical Specification section 5.3.4. Localhost binding implementation at `server.js` line 3: `const hostname = '127.0.0.1';`. Scope limitations defined in section 1.3.2.1.

#### 6.4.5.2 Network Boundary Enforcement

**Primary Security Boundary:** Operating System Routing Table

The operating system enforces an impenetrable network boundary at the kernel level through RFC 1122-compliant loopback interface handling:

**Boundary Enforcement Mechanism:**

| Access Source | Network Path | OS Action | Result |
|--------------|--------------|-----------|--------|
| Localhost processes | Loopback interface | Route to 127.0.0.1 | ✅ Allowed |
| LAN clients | External interface | No route to 127.0.0.1 | ❌ Blocked |
| Internet clients | External interface | No route to 127.0.0.1 | ❌ Blocked |
| Docker (isolated) | Container network | Separate namespace | ❌ Blocked |

**Technical Implementation:**

```javascript
// server.js line 3
const hostname = '127.0.0.1';  // Localhost binding

// server.js lines 11-14
server.listen(port, hostname, () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
});
```

**Evidence:** Network boundary architecture documented in Technical Specification section 4.3.1.1. Localhost binding implementation at `server.js` line 3. Functional requirement for localhost-only access in section 2.2.1.4.

**Trust Boundary Definition:**
- **Trusted Zone:** All processes executing on the local machine
- **Untrusted Zone:** All external networks and remote systems
- **Security Perimeter:** Operating system kernel and network stack

**Boundary Crossing Rules:**
- External → Internal: Blocked by OS routing (zero application-level checks)
- Internal → Internal: Allowed without restrictions (no application-level authorization)

**Evidence:** Trust boundary documentation in Technical Specification section 4.3. Security perimeter defined in section 5.3.4.3.

#### 6.4.6.3 Accepted Risks and Justification

**Accepted Risk: Local Malicious Processes**

**Risk Description:** Malware or malicious scripts running on the local machine can send HTTP requests to `127.0.0.1:3000` and receive responses.

**Risk Acceptance Rationale:**
1. **Broad Compromise Assumption:** If local machine is compromised with malware, attacker likely has root/admin access and can:
   - Read server source code and memory
   - Intercept system calls
   - Modify server binary
   - Access all user data regardless of application-level controls

2. **Minimal Additional Protection:** Application-level authentication provides negligible additional security when OS is compromised:
   - Malware can read config files containing credentials
   - Malware can intercept authentication tokens from memory
   - Malware can directly access data files bypassing application logic

3. **Cost-Benefit Analysis:** Implementing authentication requires:
   - API key generation and distribution infrastructure
   - Key storage and secure retrieval mechanisms
   - Validation logic and error handling in request handler
   - Key rotation and revocation procedures
   - Benefit: Minimal (only protects against already-accepted local threat)

**Evidence:** Risk acceptance documented in Technical Specification section 5.3.4.3. Security decision rationale in section 5.3.4.4. Threat model in section 4.3.

#### 6.4.6.4 Threats Not Applicable

**Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attacks:**
- **Status:** Not applicable
- **Rationale:** Loopback traffic routed internally by kernel, never traverses physical network interfaces or switches
- **Technical Justification:** RFC 1122 specifies loopback packets remain within host network stack

**Injection Attacks:**
- **SQL Injection:** No database or SQL queries
- **Command Injection:** No system command execution
- **XSS Attacks:** Static response, no user input rendered
- **Status:** Not applicable
- **Evidence:** Request object completely ignored in handler (lines 6-10 of `server.js`)

**Session Hijacking:**
- **Status:** Not applicable
- **Rationale:** No session management, cookies, or session tokens
- **Evidence:** Stateless architecture with no session store

**Evidence:** Complete threat analysis in Technical Specification section 5.3.4.3. Code review confirms request data never processed.

#### 6.4.7.2 Implementation Roadmap for Security Enhancement

**If External Access Becomes Required:**

**Step 1: Change Network Binding**
```javascript
// Change from:
const hostname = '127.0.0.1';

// To:
const hostname = '0.0.0.0';  // Listen on all interfaces
```

**Step 2: Implement API Key Authentication (Minimum)**
- Generate secure random API keys
- Store keys in environment variables or secrets manager
- Validate `Authorization` header on each request
- Return HTTP 401 Unauthorized for invalid/missing keys

**Step 3: Add HTTPS/TLS Encryption**
- Obtain SSL/TLS certificate (Let's Encrypt or commercial CA)
- Switch from `http` to `https` module
- Configure TLS 1.2+ with secure cipher suites
- Enforce HTTPS-only access

**Step 4: Deploy Behind Reverse Proxy**
- Install nginx or Apache as reverse proxy
- Configure security headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options)
- Implement rate limiting at proxy level
- Add DDoS protection

**Step 5: Implement Comprehensive Logging**
- Log all authentication attempts (success and failure)
- Log authorization decisions
- Log all API requests with timestamps
- Integrate with SIEM for security monitoring

**Evidence:** External access security requirements documented in Technical Specification section 5.3.4.4. Security enhancement roadmap in section 3.1.3.

### 6.4.9 Conclusion and Security Posture Summary

#### 6.4.9.1 Security Architecture Summary

The hao-backprop-test system implements a **minimalist security model** appropriate for local development test infrastructure:

**Primary Security Control:** Operating system-level network isolation via localhost binding (127.0.0.1)

**Application-Level Security:** Explicitly not implemented (authentication, authorization, encryption, audit logging)

**Risk Posture:** Accepted risk model where local machine trust boundary is the sole security enforcement point

**Threat Mitigation:** External network threats comprehensively mitigated; local malicious process threats explicitly accepted

#### 6.4.9.2 Appropriateness of Security Model

This security architecture is **appropriate and sufficient** for the system's classification as:
- Test infrastructure (not production system)
- Localhost-only deployment (developer workstation)
- Zero data persistence (stateless architecture)
- Minimal attack surface (15-line implementation)

The security model would be **inappropriate** if the system were:
- Exposed to external networks
- Handling sensitive or personal data
- Deployed in production environments
- Subject to compliance requirements

#### 6.4.9.3 Security Evolution Path

**Current State:** OS-level isolation only
**Required Changes for External Access:** Comprehensive security overhaul including authentication, encryption, monitoring, and infrastructure hardening
**Effort Estimate:** 10-20x code complexity increase, ongoing security maintenance overhead

**Evidence:** Security architecture justification in Technical Specification section 5.3.4. Scope limitations in section 1.3. System overview in section 1.2.

## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Monitoring Applicability Assessment

#### 6.5.1.1 Applicability Statement

**Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system.** The hao-backprop-test repository implements a minimal 15-line Node.js HTTP server designed exclusively for local integration testing purposes. This system fundamentally lacks the production deployment characteristics, operational complexity, and business criticality that would necessitate comprehensive monitoring and observability infrastructure.

The system's classification as test-only infrastructure, combined with its localhost-only deployment model (127.0.0.1:3000), developer-operated execution, and stateless architecture, renders traditional production monitoring patterns both technically infeasible and operationally unnecessary.

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 1.2.1.1 classifies system as "internal testing utility rather than a market-facing product or service." Section 5.4.1.1 explicitly states "Minimal observability suitable for test infrastructure." Complete implementation in `server.js` (15 lines total) with single logging statement at line 13.

|-----------------|-------------------|-------------|-----------|
| Metrics Collection | Prometheus, CloudWatch, StatsD | ❌ Not implemented | Test infrastructure, no SLA requirements |
| Log Aggregation | ELK Stack, Splunk, Loki | ❌ Not implemented | Developer observes stdout directly |
| Distributed Tracing | Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry | ❌ Not applicable | Single-component monolith |
| Health Checks | Dedicated /health endpoints | ❌ Not implemented | Process presence = health status |

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.2 documents comprehensive "Observability Gaps" showing all industry-standard monitoring features not implemented. Section 6.1.4.2 confirms "No metrics collection" infrastructure.

#### 6.5.1.3 System Characteristics Influencing Monitoring Strategy

**Architectural Factors:**

1. **Localhost-Only Deployment**: Server binds exclusively to 127.0.0.1, preventing external network access and eliminating need for external monitoring infrastructure
2. **Developer Presence**: Developer is present at terminal during testing, enabling immediate observation of server behavior and failures
3. **Short Feedback Loops**: Process crashes immediately visible in terminal window with stack trace output
4. **Single Machine Scope**: No distributed system complexity requiring correlation across multiple services or machines
5. **Stateless Operation**: No data persistence means no data loss monitoring, no backup verification, no storage capacity tracking
6. **Zero Dependencies**: No third-party services to monitor for availability or performance degradation

**Operational Factors:**

1. **Test Infrastructure Classification**: Not a production service requiring 24/7 uptime or SLA compliance
2. **Manual Operation**: Executed via `node server.js` command, terminated via Ctrl+C, no daemon mode
3. **Immediate Failure Detection**: Terminal displays all errors, exceptions, and process exits in real-time
4. **No External Users**: No customer impact from downtime, no user experience metrics to track
5. **Deterministic Behavior**: Static "Hello, World!" response provides predictable, easily verifiable output

**Evidence:** Localhost binding at `server.js` line 3: `const hostname = '127.0.0.1';`. Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.3 provides comprehensive "Monitoring Strategy Justification" documenting why minimal observability is acceptable. Section 4.3.1.1 details operating system-level network isolation preventing external access.

### 6.5.2 Current Observability Implementation

#### 6.5.2.1 Logging Infrastructure

**Implemented Logging:**

The system implements minimal console-based logging suitable for local development testing:

```javascript
// server.js line 13: Single log statement
console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
```

**Log Output Example:**
```
Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/
```

**Logging Characteristics:**

| Characteristic | Implementation | Description |
|---------------|----------------|-------------|
| **Frequency** | One-time at startup | Single message when server begins listening |
| **Destination** | stdout stream | Terminal output only, no file persistence |
| **Format** | Plain text | No structured logging (JSON, key-value pairs) |
| **Persistence** | Ephemeral | Exists only in terminal buffer, lost after close |

**Evidence:** Complete logging implementation at `server.js` line 13. Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.1 documents "Current Observability Implementation" with code evidence.

#### 6.5.2.2 Logging Architecture Flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Node.js Process"
        SERVER[server.js<br/>Line 13] -->|console.log| CONSOLE[Console API]
    end
    
    subgraph "Node.js Runtime"
        CONSOLE -->|Write| STDOUT[stdout Stream<br/>File Descriptor 1]
    end
    
    subgraph "Operating System"
        STDOUT -->|OS Pipes| TERMINAL[Terminal Display<br/>TTY Device]
    end
    
    subgraph "Log Lifecycle"
        TERMINAL -->|Scroll Buffer| MEMORY[Terminal Memory Buffer<br/>Limited Capacity]
        MEMORY -.->|Terminal Close| LOST[❌ Data Lost<br/>No Persistence]
    end
    
    style SERVER fill:#4CAF50
    style STDOUT fill:#2196F3
    style TERMINAL fill:#FFC107
    style LOST fill:#F44336
```

**Logging Flow Analysis:**

1. **Log Generation**: `console.log()` call at server startup (line 13)
2. **Console API**: Node.js console API receives log message
3. **Stream Writing**: Message written to stdout stream (file descriptor 1)
4. **OS Piping**: Operating system pipes stdout to terminal emulator
5. **Terminal Display**: Message appears in terminal window
6. **Buffer Storage**: Terminal stores message in scrollback buffer (limited capacity)
7. **Ephemeral Lifecycle**: Data lost when terminal closes or buffer overflows

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.2.1 documents "Logging Architecture" with detailed flow diagram. stdout stream behavior is standard Node.js console.log implementation.

### 6.5.6 Justification and Risk Acceptance

#### 6.5.6.1 Why Minimal Monitoring is Appropriate

**Scope-Based Justification:**

The minimal monitoring approach (single console.log statement, manual operation) is appropriate and justified for this system's scope:

**Justification Factors:**

| Factor | Description | Monitoring Impact |
|--------|-------------|------------------|
| **Test Infrastructure** | Not production service | No SLA monitoring needed |
| **Developer Presence** | Developer at terminal during testing | Immediate failure visibility without instrumentation |
| **Localhost Deployment** | 127.0.0.1 binding | Cannot be monitored externally |
| **Stateless Architecture** | No data persistence | No data loss monitoring needed |
| **Zero Dependencies** | No external services | No dependency health monitoring needed |
| **Short-Lived Execution** | Started for testing, stopped when done | No long-term trend analysis needed |
| **Single User** | One developer operator | No multi-user coordination or alerting needed |

**Cost-Benefit Analysis:**

| **No Historical Data** | Cannot analyze performance trends | High | Low | Performance already exceeds requirements |
| **No Capacity Planning** | Cannot predict future resource needs | High | None | Test infrastructure with fixed workload |

### 6.5.7 Future Monitoring Roadmap

#### 6.5.7.1 Phase 1: Basic Observability (If Needed)

**Estimated Effort:** 4-8 hours  
**Prerequisites:** System scope expansion beyond localhost testing

**Implementation Steps:**

| Step | Task | Effort | Output |
|------|------|--------|--------|
| 1 | Add request logging | 1-2 hours | Log all HTTP requests with method, path, timestamp |
| 2 | Add error handling | 2-3 hours | Try-catch blocks, process error handlers |
| 3 | Add health endpoint | 1 hour | `GET /health` returns 200 OK with status |
| 4 | Environment variables | 1-2 hours | Configurable host and port via process.env |

**Implementation Example:**

```javascript
// Phase 1: Basic observability enhancements (not currently implemented)

const http = require('http');

// Environment variable support
const hostname = process.env.HOST || '127.0.0.1';
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  // Request logging
  const timestamp = new Date().toISOString();
  console.log(`[${timestamp}] ${req.method} ${req.url}`);
  
  try {
    // Health check endpoint
    if (req.url === '/health') {
      res.statusCode = 200;
      res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'healthy', timestamp }));
      return;
    }
    
    // Default endpoint
    res.statusCode = 200;
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
    res.end('Hello, World!\n');
    
    // Response logging
    console.log(`[${timestamp}] Response: ${res.statusCode}`);
  } catch (err) {
    // Error logging
    console.error(`[${timestamp}] ERROR:`, err);
    res.statusCode = 500;
    res.end('Internal Server Error');
  }
});

// Server error handling
server.on('error', (err) => {
  console.error('Server error:', err.message);
  if (err.code === 'EADDRINUSE') {
    console.error(`Port ${port} already in use`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
});

// Process error handling
process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => {
  console.error('Uncaught exception:', err);
  server.close(() => process.exit(1));
});

server.listen(port, hostname, () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
  console.log(`Health check: http://${hostname}:${port}/health`);
});
```

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.3 provides "Recommended implementation path" for production observability including request logging, error tracking, and health endpoints.

#### 6.5.7.2 Phase 2: Metrics and Monitoring (If Production Deployment)

**Estimated Effort:** 20-40 hours  
**Prerequisites:** Phase 1 complete, production deployment planned

**Implementation Steps:**

| Step | Technology | Effort | Purpose |
|------|-----------|--------|---------|
| 1 | Install prom-client | 2-4 hours | Prometheus metrics client library |
| 2 | Instrument application | 4-8 hours | Add metrics collection to code |
| 3 | Create /metrics endpoint | 2-4 hours | Expose metrics for Prometheus scraping |
| 4 | Deploy Prometheus server | 4-8 hours | Set up metrics storage and querying |
| 5 | Configure Grafana | 4-8 hours | Create dashboards for visualization |
| 6 | Set up alert rules | 4-8 hours | Define alerting thresholds |

**Metrics Implementation Example:**

```javascript
// Phase 2: Prometheus metrics (not currently implemented)

const http = require('http');
const promClient = require('prom-client');

// Create Prometheus registry
const register = new promClient.Registry();

// Default metrics (CPU, memory, etc.)
promClient.collectDefaultMetrics({ register });

// Custom metrics
const httpRequestDuration = new promClient.Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'Duration of HTTP requests in seconds',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
  registers: [register]
});

const httpRequestTotal = new promClient.Counter({
  name: 'http_requests_total',
  help: 'Total number of HTTP requests',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
  registers: [register]
});

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const start = Date.now();
  
  // Metrics endpoint
  if (req.url === '/metrics') {
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', register.contentType);
    res.end(register.metrics());
    return;
  }
  
  // Health check endpoint
  if (req.url === '/health') {
    res.statusCode = 200;
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'healthy' }));
    
    // Record metrics
    const duration = (Date.now() - start) / 1000;
    httpRequestDuration.observe({ method: req.method, route: '/health', status: 200 }, duration);
    httpRequestTotal.inc({ method: req.method, route: '/health', status: 200 });
    return;
  }
  
  // Default endpoint
  res.statusCode = 200;
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
  res.end('Hello, World!\n');
  
  // Record metrics
  const duration = (Date.now() - start) / 1000;
  httpRequestDuration.observe({ method: req.method, route: '/', status: 200 }, duration);
  httpRequestTotal.inc({ method: req.method, route: '/', status: 200 });
});

const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
server.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${port}`);
  console.log(`Metrics available at http://localhost:${port}/metrics`);
});
```

**Evidence:** Technical Specification Section 5.4.1.3 recommends "Export metrics: Prometheus metrics endpoint for Grafana dashboards" as part of production observability roadmap.
